newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU official tells Euro MPs no BSE cover-up.
newsitem.headline: EU official tells Euro MPs no BSE cover-up.

text.p: The European Commission's chief agriculture official on Tuesday denied to the European parliament any cover-up over the risk to public health posed by mad cow disease.

The French daily newspaper Liberation alleged on September 2 that the official, Frenchman Guy Legras, had suggested in 1993 that EU veterinary experts avoid discussing the danger to human health because it would undermine the beef market.

"Neither the Commission nor DG VI (Directorate General for Agriculture) conducted such a policy," Legras told a parliamentary committee of inquiry into Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) - the medical name for mad cow disease.

Legras, who heads the agriculture directorate, said that a remark by former EU Farm Commissioner Ray MacSharry was the cause of a controversial memo suggesting that all discussion of BSE be kept out of scientific meetings.
At a weekly meeting with MacSharry, Legras said he heard the Commissioner say, "I am fed up with BSE, I do not want to hear any more of it."
Legras told the inquiry: "I did not take it seriously, I just assumed it was an off the cuff remark."

He said that he could now see no other explanation for a memo written by another senior Commission agricultural official, Fernando Mansito, shortly afterwards on October 10, 1990, which said that discussion of BSE should be kept out of meetings "because the press tend to exaggerate".
Legras reiterated it was impossible for the EU's executive Commission to hide scientific research as it is is published independently.
In a detailed preliminary statement, Legras said the Commission had consistently followed the advice of the EU scientific committee but on several occasions this had been rejected by member states.
Most recently, member states rejected a Commission proposal in July for an EU-wide ban on the use of suspect sheep tissue, saying the risk of sheep catching BSE was very slight.
Legras claimed the EU had done the best it could to protect public health but there was a large degree of uncertainty about the disease and there were still doubts about its cause.
"Everyone is saying that it is bone meal but I can't be sure. There was uncertainty over the whole issue and there still is," he said in reply to a question.
Legras deplored that initially there were only 12 EU veterinary inspectors which made it impossible to carry out adequate controls in member states.
After he had complained many times about the "catastrophic situation" the number of inspectors was raised to 30 but this was still far short of the 100 requested.
Legras stressed that it was up to member states to apply EU rules. The Commission's role was to check that this was done.
"It can only work if there is a sufficient counterweight (in Brussels). That does not exist today," he said, adding that financial penalties were needed to ensure compliance.
An EU inspectors' report on Britain in 1994 found that BSE controls were generally satisfactory although improvements were needed on the identification of cattle, he said.
